2828.tone: Soon 2022 classes Kwényï as tonal in Hyman's broad sense but marginally so: a two-way pitch contrast in some monosyllabic minimal pairs, tone-bearing unit the syllable, narrow pitch range (150-250 Hz), low functional load, possibly privative, no grammatical function, probably being lost; sec. 4.5 calls Kwényï 'this tonal New Caledonian language' with 'a hybrid system where stress and tone coexist' and no evidence of stress-tone interaction. For nuclear Numèè (Goro/Touaourou, nucl1484) Lionnet 2025 sec. 6.2 (pp. 39-40) describes a culminative lexical register/downstep contrast on the mora and argues it is NOT accentual ('Neither of Hyman's (2006) inviolable criteria' is met), classes Numèè among 'bona fide tonal languages' and gives no stress-placement statement; Lionnet excludes Kwényï because 'it differs markedly with respect to its prosodic system (Rivierre 1973: 154)', and carries Rivierre's remark that the two varieties' 'sentence melody is astonishingly opposite'.

2831.dq: The syllable structure of Nyah Kur words is rendered extremely complex by extensive Thai loans ... If we confine ourselves to native Nyah Kur words, they may be either 1) monosyllabic ... or 2) disyllabic, consisting of an unstressed presyllable of shape /CV-/, where /V/ is always /ə/, plus a stressed syllable having one of the shapes represented in 1) above.
2831.dloc: MKS 16-17 p.56 (page re-rendered and read directly by C), sec. 1.3.3 'Syllable Structure' under 1.3 'Nyah Kur of Ban Wang Ai Pho'; register/pitch remarks p.51, sec. 1.3.2 Vowels, note 2. Parallel Burmese Mon statement p.39 sec. 1.1.3. Bunphan 1982 ch. 2 p.8 (re-read by C).
2831.prule: Fixed final, quantity-insensitive: native Nyah Kur words are either monosyllables (the one syllable stressed) or disyllables consisting of 'an unstressed presyllable of shape /CV-/, where /V/ is always /ə/, plus a stressed syllable having one of the shapes represented in 1) above', so stress falls on the last syllable of the word. The stressed syllable may be V́C or V́V(C) (short vowel + obligatory coda, or long vowel/diphthong with optional coda), so no weight test decides the position; the presyllable is a structural constant (/Cə-/), not a weight class that could compete for stress. Extensionally identical to 'stress the full (major) syllable' because a native word has exactly one full syllable and it is final; the source words it by word shape and position, as in the parallel Burmese Mon statement (sec. 1.1.3: 'a single stressed syllable... or... such a syllable preceded by an unstressed presyllable of the structure /CV-/').

2831.tone: Not a tone language. Huffman p.51: 'Since Nyah Kur, like Mon, is a register language, all short and long vowels and diphthongs occur on both sets'; note 2: "'Light' words with long vowels are accompanied by a (as yet non-contrastive) high-falling tone, while 'heavy' words with long vowels are characterized by a low level tone, lax quality, and breathiness which carries throughout the word. Short vowels ending in stops, whether light or heavy, have a high level tone." Then (pp.51-52): 'Thai loans with short vowels and rising tone seem to retain their rising tone in Nyah Kur'. Pitch is an accompaniment of register, not a stress or tone rule; Huffman's acute is a stress mark, distinct from the grave register mark. Bunphan 1982 p.8 likewise describes two registers (clear voice ' vs breathy voice `), 'ความแตกต่างของลักษณะน้ำเสียงทั้ง 2 จะปรากฏให้เห็นชัดเจนในพยางค์หลักของคำเท่านั้น' [the difference between the two registers shows clearly only in the major syllable of the word].

2833.dq: It should be noted that in Mangde tone moves to the first syllable of a word if negative marker <ma-> precedes verbs or adjectives. Native speakers of Mangde also have the intuition that the first syllable of the word is somehow more prominent.
2833.prule: Two-way register tone (H/L) on the word-initial syllable, largely predictable from onset voicing and contrastive only after sonorants and the palatal fricative; the contrast is nearly neutralised from the second syllable on. No stress rule is stated.
2833.quote: The initial of every Mangde syllable is obligatorily marked for high or low tone. Therefore, we computed pitch measurements based on initial tone of the word and the means of pitch peak and average. The mean pitch for initial syllables with high tone was 197 Hz while the mean pitch for initial syllables with low tone was 165 Hz. By the second syllable, these tonal differences have nearly neutralized. High toned words had a mean pitch of 188 for second syllable and low-toned words had a mean pitch of 179 Hz for second syllable. It should be noted that in Mangde tone moves to the first syllable…
2833.idn: Mangde / Mangdebi-kha ('Nyenkha, Ngenkha, Henkha, Mangdekha) as spoken at Tshangkha village, Tangsibji gewog, Trongsa Dzongkhag (Nishida 2009 calls it the ツァンカ (Tsankha) 方言 'Tsangkha dialect' of Mangdebi-kha) (a named variety of the language); data: Fieldwork at Tshangkha village, Tangsibji gewog, Trongsa district…
2833.tone: Register-tone description: every syllable initial is H or L; F0 means 197 Hz (H) vs 165 Hz (L) on first syllables, 188 vs 179 Hz on second syllables ('nearly neutralized'); tone predictable from obstruent voicing except after sonorants and the voiceless palatal fricative, where it is contrastive (minimal pairs Hmi 'thing' / Lmi 'person', Hwang 'blessing' / Lwang 'hole', Hra 'hair' / Lra 'root'). The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the paper; the only prominence remark is the hedged speaker-intuition sentence about the first syllable. Nishida 2009 (Chiba, Japanese, sec. 3.4 p. 69) adds word melodies: first syllable H -> following syllables L; first syllable L -> second H, third L; phonemic status of the register left open there. Nishida's KAKEN 23720195 report lists a 'pitch accent system of compounding words' for the Tshangkha variety without stating a rule.

2834.dq: The Word rank is defined as the rank whose units have a structure in terms of Syllables and function in the Intonation Group. The Word in Nyeu has components of stress and pitch. [p. 29] ... 3.3 Word Stress. Stress in Nyeu is predictable as follows [p. 33]
2834.dloc: Ch. III 'The Word': sec. 3.1 General Definition p. 29; sec. 3.3 Word Stress p. 33
2834.prule: Primary stress is predictable and falls on the last syllable of the phonological word (1-3 syllables): monosyllables; disyllables of Type A (presyllable Cə + major syllable), Type B (closed or long-vowel syllable + major) and ordinary Type C (two free syllables); trisyllables of Types A and B ('in trisyllabic words the primary stress is always on the last syllable of a word'). The one stated exception: disyllabic Type C words whose first syllable ends in ʔ or h have primary stress on the first syllable and secondary on the last ([ˈdiəʔ ˌmat] 'tears', [ˈmuh ˌmat] 'looks, one's face'). Stress is not marked in phonemic writing.
2834.srule: Secondary stress falls on the non-final full syllable; presyllables (Cə) are unstressed, so a word carries at most one secondary stress (p. 29). Disyllabic Type B (closed or long-vowel first syllable) and Type C (two free syllables): secondary on the first syllable ([ˌpiŋˈwaːj] 'spider', [ˌɲitˈsuːt] 'silk cloth'); disyllabic Type A (Cə + major): none ([təˈpaj]). Trisyllabic Type A (Cə.CV(C).CV(C)): secondary on the second syllable ([kəˌpoːŋˈloːŋ] 'a balloon'); Type B (CV(C).Cə.CV(C)): on the first ([ˌkamsəˈnaː] 'a bow'). In the ʔ/h-coda Type C class (initial primary) secondary is on the last syllable (['diəʔˌmat] 'tears').

2835.heavy: the stem syllable 'wenn diese gedehnt' / disyllabic stems 'ohne gelängten Vokal' do not count: a syllable with a lengthened (long) vowel. The 'Zu 1.' examples include stems whose accented syllable precedes a nasal+consonant cluster (umugunda 'Garten, Feld', umununsi 'Gestank', umuvombi 'Arbeiter') beside inherently long vowels (umwaha 'Jahr', umwotho 'Feuer'), so pre-NC lengthening counts as 'gedehnt'; accent/length diacritics are garbled in the excerpt layer
2835.dflt: monosyllabic stems and short-vowelled disyllabic stems: accent on the preceding prefix syllable ('rückt der Akzent auf die vorangehende Präfixsilbe'), tending even onto the first prefix syllable; trisyllabic stems keep the stem-initial (antepenult) accent; words of more than four syllables take the penult; strengthened subjunctive: antepenult with rising tone
2835.prule: Main accent (Hauptakzent, acute) on the stem syllable when that syllable is long ('gedehnt') or when the stem is trisyllabic; with monosyllabic stems and disyllabic stems without a lengthened vowel the accent retracts onto the preceding prefix syllable, 'sogar' tending onto the first prefix syllable; words of more than four syllables take the penult. Simple verbs follow the same rule (§ 209); extended verb forms are placed by morphology (object prefix -> penult; suffixed simple/causative/passive verbs -> penult with high tone; certain forms -> final syllable with high tone, penult low; strengthened subjunctive -> antepenult with rising tone, monosyllabic/causative/passive verbs -> penult; negative -tha- and temporal -a- carry a secondary accent). Net placement: a long (incl. pre-NC) stem-initial syllable takes the accent (heavy penult in disyllabic stems), otherwise antepenult or further left; the accented syllable carries H or rising tone. Hedged throughout ('scheinen', 'Neigung', 'in der Regel', 'meist', 'wenn ich recht gehört habe').
2835.srule: A secondary accent (Nebenakzent, grave) is recognised beside the main accent and placed morphologically, not rhythmically: on the first syllable of certain derived nouns that keep their main accent (p. 80, üwašíphalo); in verbs on the negation particle -tha- ('meist', pp. 81-83) and on the inserted temporal particle -a- (with high tone, p. 82); in negated four-syllable subjunctives -tha- and the penult are both accented, 'gleich stark' (p. 83). No alternating/rhythmic secondary stress is described.

2840.tone: The source calls the system 'tone' throughout and never uses 'stress' or 'accent' for Nyoro (a full-text search of the English Kaji texts: no hits outside a bibliography entry). It is a two-pattern culminative system (one lexical H per nominal, confined to the final two syllables, penult vs final), with obligatory H anticipation before pause and no toneless words. In the Japanese chapter Kaji explicitly flags the naming question: 'こういった言語を声調言語と呼ぶかどうかは大きな問題があるが、ここではその問題には立ち入らず、近隣言語との関係上、声調と呼ぶことにする。' (ILCAA ch. 7 p. 141). Summary (39) p. 160: nominals show the so-called 2型 with only two patterns however long the word; TBU is the syllable and tone behaves identically on light and heavy syllables; final-syllable H anticipation occurs in isolation.

2844.tone: Two-way word-level tone ('accent') contrast: high = level pitch on the word, low = falling pitch on the last syllable; an acute accent is written on the final vowel of high-pitch words only where a low-pitch minimal pair exists. 2851.prule: No stress rule. Okiek (Kalenjin) is a tone language; Rottland finds no phonemic stress (Druckakzent) in his recordings and does not mark it; phonetically prominent syllables are always ones bearing non-low tone. In Heine's (1973) Sogoo Okiek vocabulary, where stress and tone are marked independently, stress goes with high or falling tone and is 'weiter nicht vorhersagbar' (otherwise not predictable). No positional (edge-counted) or weight-based rule is stated by any source.

2851.tone: Rottland 1982 p. 78 reports Tucker's (1964: 457) analysis of Kalenjin with three level tones (Hoch, Mittel, Tief) plus a falling tone, three positionally conditioned rising tones and downstep; Rottland's own view (p. 79): 'Auch sonst habe ich im Kalenjin kein Indiz für eine mittlere phonemische Tonebene gefunden' (two level tones). He treats the earlier authors' 'stress' as a correlate of high/rising tone. The two open modern Okiek grammars are tonal and silent on word stress: Ochieng 2025 (Nessuit Okiek) sec. 2.3.1 p. 44: 'There are two distinct tones i.e., a high tone (H)... and a low tone (L)... Nouns in syntactic positions i.e., in phrases and clauses are marked for case by tone... Nouns in isolation have a randomly varying lexical tone pattern'; Micheli 2018 (Mariashoni Ogiek) sec. 2.3 p. 10: 'Ogiek seems to recognize at least three different tones: H, M, L.' Sister language Akie (mosi1247, not this record): König/Heine/Legère 2015 p. 25 'Stress, or pitch accent, clearly exists but does not appear to phonologically distinctive.'

tn.quote: Auch sonst habe ich im Kalenjin kein Indiz für eine mittlere phonemische Tonebene gefunden. … Mit ihnen unterscheide ich vier Toneme: Tief, Hoch, Fallend, Steigend. Was den 'downstep' angeht, so ergab sich mit vielen Informanten der Eindruck eines sehr geringen Niveauunterschiedes zwischen hohen und nicht-hohen Tönen, so daß man leicht geneigt ist, herabgesetzte Hochtöne zu notieren. Nirgendwo jedoch ergab sich bisher die Notwendigkeit, größere von kleineren Tonintervallen phonemisch zu unterscheiden.
tn.translation: Nor have I otherwise found in Kalenjin any indication of a mid phonemic tone level. ... With them [Toweett and Creider, on Kipsikiis and Nandi] I distinguish four tonemes: low, high, falling, rising. As regards 'downstep', with many informants there was the impression of a very small difference in level between high and non-high tones, so that one is easily inclined to note lowered high tones. Nowhere, however, has the need so far arisen to distinguish larger from smaller tone intervals phonemically.

2854.prule: No stress rule is established for this language. Segert 3.5.1: for Old Aramaic stress (its intensity, position and changes) only 'a few indications' can be determined from the directly transmitted (unvocalised consonantal) texts; the set of rules comes from the Babylonian- and Tiberian-pointed Bible texts and its reality 'depends on the reliability of the Masoretic tradition'. The positive rule of 3.5.2 (main stress on the last syllable in most words; penultimate main stress only in some word classes and forms, listed in 3.5.3) is explicitly scoped 'nach der masoretischen tiberischen Überlieferung', i.e. the Tiberian reading tradition of Biblical Aramaic (Glottolog impe1235), a millennium-plus later than the olda1245 inscriptions.
2854.srule: Segert 1975 sec. 3.5.6 'Der Nebenton' (p. 105): in the Tiberian Masoretic reading tradition of Biblical Aramaic a secondary stress (Nebenton) is indicated by the meteg or another accent sign; no placement rule is given, and Segert adds that for the grammar only the vowel quantity often associated with it (especially of the qameṣ) matters (cf. 2.5.5.3 on the meteg sign and the syllable table in 'Die Silbenbildung', p. 101, class 'II. mit Nebenton'). For the Old Aramaic inscriptions themselves nothing is said about secondary stress (3.5.1: only 'einige Indizien' about stress at all).

2854.cfw: Segert 1975 states that the unvocalized Old Aramaic texts yield only indirect clues to stress and that the known rules (mainly final stress, penultimate in certain word classes) come from the much later Masoretic vocalization of Biblical Aramaic, while Creason 2004 reconstructs the same final-or-penultimate pattern for Proto-Aramaic and Folmer 2011 gives no rule for this stage, so leaving the record undetermined is the clear reading on a small number of sources with no real disagreement.
